findings.headline: Your monthly maintenance fee is an extreme outlier.
findings.body: At $25.00, your maintenance fee is 4.6x the $5.48 peer median and 4x the $6.00 national median — the highest in the comparison set and flagged as an extreme outlier. Only four peer banks publish this fee, so the cohort is thin, but the national benchmark tells the same story. A recurring $25 charge is the most visible number on your schedule, twelve times a year.

findings.stat_label: your NSF fee vs national median
findings.headline: Your NSF fee matches local peers — and doubles the national benchmark.
findings.body: At $30, NSF sits exactly at the peer median of 13 comparable banks, so locally you are at market. Nationally, the median has fallen to $15 as institutions retire returned-item fees under regulatory scrutiny. Being at local market on a fee the industry is abandoning is a position worth revisiting before the local market moves too.

findings.headline: You are below market on service fees — quietly.
findings.body: Overdraft-protection transfers ($3 vs an $8 median), stop payments ($25 vs $30, 44th percentile), and cashier's checks ($4 vs $5) all run below the peer median. Everywhere else — wires, card replacement, deposited item returns — you sit at or within a dollar of market. The schedule is essentially at-market with one large exception at the top.

exec_narrative: Net position: Riverside Bank of Dublin prices almost everything at or slightly below market — penalty fees, wires, and card services all track the medians of its 35-bank cohort — with one dominant exception: a $25 monthly maintenance fee that is more than four times both the peer and national medians and flagged as an extreme outlier. Because maintenance is recurring and universal where most fees are episodic, that single line likely outweighs every other pricing decision on the schedule combined. The three findings above are the agenda for a one-hour pricing conversation.

callouts.title: Monthly maintenance — $25.00
callouts.stat: Peer median $5.48 · 100th percentile · n=4 · national median $6.00 · flagged: extreme outlier (>2x median)
callouts.body: Four publishing peers make for a thin local comparison, but the national median of $6 confirms the picture: $25 is a premium-tier maintenance fee on a community-bank schedule. If it funds a genuinely premium account with offset conditions, document and market that. If it is legacy pricing, it is the single most conspicuous line a prospective customer — or a fee survey — will find.

callouts.title: NSF / returned item — $30.00
callouts.stat: Peer median $30.00 · national median $15.00 · 77th percentile · n=13
callouts.body: You are at the local median, which is a defensible position today. But the national median is half that, and the direction of travel is one way: large banks have largely eliminated NSF fees and the pressure is migrating down-market. Deciding now whether Riverside follows or holds — rather than waiting for the cohort median to fall around you — keeps this a choice instead of a reaction.

callouts.title: Incoming domestic wire — $20.00
callouts.body: Only three peers publish this fee, so read the percentile loosely — but charging the top of the range to receive money is friction aimed at your most attractive customers, and the $5 premium over the median earns little revenue for the signal it sends.

callouts.title: Service fees — priced below market, marketed nowhere
callouts.stat: OD protection transfer $3 vs $8 median · Stop payment $25 vs $30 (P44) · Cashier's check $4 vs $5
callouts.body: Three customer-facing service fees run below the cohort. If deliberate, they are a marketing claim your competitors' own published schedules substantiate — 'lower service fees than most banks in your market.' If not deliberate, they are quiet margin. Today they are neither, because nobody knows about them.

context_narrative:
Two currents define the fee landscape your schedule competes in. First, the retreat from NSF: large banks have largely eliminated returned-item fees, and the national median has fallen to $15 — half your posted fee, even though your local 13-bank cohort still clusters at $30. Second, published fee schedules have become public documents: scraped, compared, and surfaced in fee surveys, which converts every outlier line — like a $25 maintenance fee against a $6 national median — into a small reputational bet.

Small community banks compete on relationships and local trust, not brand gravity, and their fee schedules are read accordingly: customers expect neighborly pricing and notice when a line breaks that expectation. For Riverside Bank of Dublin the leverage is unusually concentrated — the schedule is already at or below market almost everywhere, so the work is not a broad repricing but a single decision on the maintenance fee, paired with actually advertising the service fees already priced below the market's own published numbers.
